title: UK Landscapes & Geomorphic Processes
text: Describe two ways in which freeze-thaw weathering shapes upland UK landscapes.

subject: computer-science-aqa
title: Searching Algorithms: Linear and Binary Search
text: Explain what is meant by 'time efficiency' when comparing algorithms. Describe how the time efficiency of linear search and binary search differ as the size of the dataset increases.

subject: computer-science-aqa
title: Sorting Algorithms: Bubble Sort and Merge Sort

subject: hospitality-catering

subject: business
title: Managing Quality and the Sales Process

Positive impacts:

Negative impacts:

subject: business
title: The Role of Business Enterprise
text: Other than through branding, discuss a method a business can use to add value to its product or service.
marks:
Award up to 3 marks for understanding/application and up to 3 marks for analysis.
One way a business could add value is by offering increased convenience for the customer (1). This means consumers are seeking increased convenience in their purchases and often value this over price (1). As such, consumers are more likely to buy from the business offering more convenience than a competing business and may also be prepared to pay more for a similar product or service (1).
Another way of adding value is to have a clear unique selling point (USP) (1). This helps encourage sales as customers are offered something additional or different to the product or service offered by a competing business (1). As a result, customers will be attracted to the product or service with a clear USP and may be more willing to buy it rather than from a competitor (1).

subject: business
title: Product
text: Discuss the benefit to a business from using the design mix when developing new products.
marks:
Award up to 3 marks for understanding (UND) and up to 3 marks for analysis (AN).

Arguments for:
• The business will be known as a reputable brand/product due to its functionality (1). This means the product is fit for purpose, meets customer needs, and improves user satisfaction (1). Therefore, customers will be more likely to repeat purchase and stay loyal, making the product profitable (1).
• The business will have product appeal due to good design/aesthetics (1). Because by enhancing the product’s appearance, it makes it more attractive to customers (1). As a result, increasing sales potential (1).

Arguments against / limitations:
• The design mix may increase production costs if a business tries to maximise all three elements.
• Focusing too much on aesthetics may mean the product does not function well.
• Competitors may copy the design quickly, reducing the advantage.

For top marks, candidates should weigh both sides and reach a justified conclusion.

subject: separate-sciences-edexcel
title: Genetics: DNA, Inheritance and Punnett Squares
text:
Gregor Mendel proposed the principles of inheritance from his pea plant experiments, but his ideas were not accepted for many years after publication.
Evaluate reasons why Mendel's work was initially ignored, and why it was later accepted.
marks:
Top band: Argues both sides. Reasons for initial rejection: Mendel was an obscure monk with no formal scientific position; his work was published in a minor journal; the mathematical approach was unfamiliar to biologists of the time; there was no known mechanism to explain how 'factors' were passed on. Reasons for later acceptance: discovery of chromosomes and meiosis provided the physical mechanism for Mendel's ratios; scientists re-reading his paper in the early 1900s (de Vries, Correns, von Tschermak) independently reproduced his results; the chromosome theory unified his ratios with observable cell biology. Balanced conclusion with explicit criteria. (6 marks)
Upper-mid band: Both sides argued with specific points; conclusion present. (4–5 marks)
Lower-mid band: Points listed rather than evaluated; limited weighing of evidence. (2–3 marks)
Low band: One side described. (1 mark)

subject: separate-sciences-edexcel
title: Cell Structure, Microscopy and Specialised Cells
text: Describe how you would use a light microscope to prepare and view a sample of cheek cells. Include how to obtain a clear, well-focused image.

Control variable stated (e.g. same stain concentration). (6 marks)

Lower-mid band: Several steps present but gaps in method (e.g. no mention of stain or air bubble prevention). (2–3 marks)

subject: separate-sciences-edexcel
title: Enzymes, Transport and Food Tests
text: A student investigates the effect of temperature on amylase activity. Describe how she should carry out a fair investigation, including how to measure the rate of reaction.

(6 marks)

Uses correct terminology throughout. (6 marks)

Top band: Restriction enzyme used to cut desired gene from donor DNA at specific base sequences, producing sticky ends; same restriction enzyme cuts the bacterial plasmid (vector); the gene is inserted into the plasmid; ligase joins the complementary sticky ends, forming a recombinant plasmid; recombinant plasmid introduced into a host bacterium; bacterium replicates and expresses the new gene, producing the desired protein. (6 marks)

Against: reduces genetic variation (inbreeding risk); slow process (many generations); cannot introduce traits from unrelated species. For genetic engineering: faster, more precise, can insert any gene including from different kingdoms (e.g. Bt crops, insulin-producing bacteria); Against: public and ethical concerns about 'playing with nature'; potential ecological effects of GM crops; expensive. Conclusion states criteria for judgement (e.g. speed, safety, ethics) and makes an explicit decision. (6 marks)

subject: business-edexcel
title: Interpreting Business Data
text: Analyse why a business that sees rising sales revenue might still be in a weakening competitive position.
marks:
Award up to 3 marks per analytical point (1 for a statement, 1 for development, 1 for further development or contextualisation).

Acceptable points:
- Rising revenue can mask a falling market share. If the total market is growing faster than the business, competitors are capturing most of the new customers — the business is growing, but losing ground relatively.
- Rising revenue does not guarantee rising profit. If costs have risen faster than revenue (e.g. higher supplier prices, wage increases), net profit margin will fall even as headline sales grow.
- Revenue growth can be achieved by cutting prices, which increases volume but reduces margins. The business looks busier but is less financially healthy per sale.

Mark the best two analytical chains.

subject: business-edexcel
title: Stock Control and Working with Suppliers
text: Discuss how good supplier relationships can benefit a growing business.
marks:
Award up to 3 marks per point (1 for a statement, 1 for a first development, 1 for a second development). No case-study context is required for this question type.

Acceptable points include:
- Reliable delivery schedules mean a business can plan production confidently, avoiding costly stoppages. This keeps output consistent and protects customer satisfaction.
- Trusted long-term suppliers may offer preferential pricing or priority delivery, reducing input costs and improving profit margins over time.
- High-quality inputs from a dependable supplier reduce defects and returns, protecting the business’s reputation with customers.

Option A ARR: Total profit = £85,000 − £50,000 = £35,000. Average annual profit = £35,000 ÷ 5 = £7,000. ARR = (£7,000 ÷ £50,000) × 100 = 14.00%.

Option B ARR: Total profit = £36,000 − £20,000 = £16,000. Average annual profit = £16,000 ÷ 4 = £4,000. ARR = (£4,000 ÷ £20,000) × 100 = 20.00%.

Option B has a higher ARR (20% vs 14%). Contextual development: the pop-up stall generates a better return per pound invested. subject: geography-eduqas
title: Your Fieldwork Approach for 2028: Transects and Place
text: Compare the quantitative and qualitative techniques you could use in a 'place' enquiry comparing two contrasting urban neighbourhoods.
marks:
Up to 4 marks for a balanced comparison. Indicative content:
• Quantitative: measured data such as housing density counts or traffic counts, producing numbers that can be averaged and graphed (1-2 marks).
• Qualitative: bi-polar surveys scoring features like cleanliness or safety, or annotated photographs capturing impressions (1-2 marks).
• Comparison point: both types are needed to build a full picture of each neighbourhood's identity, since numbers alone miss resident opinion.
